rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran leaves the Spirit's identity unsettled, saying that human knowledge of it is limited.
rows.anchor: Even the Quran does not give a definitive explanation, responding instead by saying, They ask thee about the Spirit.

rows.speaker: al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī observes that the Quran uses “the Spirit” with multiple meanings.
rows.anchor: ‘The Spirit’ is found in the Quran with many meanings

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies the Spirit as the Archangel Gabriel, as in the title Trustworthy Spirit.
rows.anchor: some say it refers to the Archangel Gabriel (IK, Q, R)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the Spirit as God's first creature, which may or may not be Gabriel.
rows.anchor: Others say that here the Spirit does not specify a particular angel, but the first creature created by God (Q, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels may be the noblest angels, including the recorders of each person's deeds, or all angels.
rows.anchor: responsible for recording the deeds of each individual (see commentary on 82:10–12), or all angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaffan, translated “in rows,” can also mean “in a row.”
rows.anchor: In rows, translating ṣaffan, could also mean “in a row.”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: One reading places the Spirit and angels together in one row.
rows.anchor: Some read the verse to mean that the Spirit and the angels stand in a single row

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Another reading has the Spirit standing alone and the angels in a row.
rows.anchor: others take it to mean that the Spirit stands alone, while the angels stand in a row (Āl).

rows.speaker: Āl, R
rows.claim: Some read the angels as standing in many rows, as in the description of 89:22.
rows.anchor: some read ṣaffan to mean that the angels stand in many rows (Āl, R).

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, R
rows.claim: The permitted speaker may be an intercessor whom God allows to intercede for others, paralleling 2:255.
rows.anchor: is interpreted as a reference to those whom God permits to intercede on behalf of others

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, R
rows.claim: On this reading, the speaker who speaks aright is an intercessor who speaks rightly about those for whom he intercedes.
rows.anchor: they will only be able to speak aright about those for whom they intercede (Āl, Q, R).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the one who speaks aright as a prophet.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that this refers to the prophets (IK).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the speaker as someone who professes that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: who speaks aright means those who say,“There is no god but God” (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A syntactic alternative ends the exception after God's permission and says that the permitted speaker then necessarily speaks aright.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that the verse should be read,“save one whom the Compassionate permits. And he speaks aright,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is probably the earliest-revealed Quranic account of Moses; it assumes Arabs knew the story and warns the Prophet and his followers about the fate of unjust rulers such as Makkah's rulers.
rows.anchor: This is most likely the first account of Moses in the chronological order of revelation. As it occurred early in the Makkan period

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭuwā may be a proper name for the valley below Mount Sinai where Moses first heard God's Voice.
rows.anchor: Ṭuwā is either a proper name for the valley said to lie just below Mt. Sinai, where Moses first heard the Voice of God

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, Ṭuwā may derive from ṭawā or ṭayya, “to roll up,” describing a valley wrapped in sanctity or sanctified twice.
rows.anchor: a term derived from the verb ṭawā/ṭayya, “to roll up,” meaning that the valley is wrapped in sanctity or that it is sanctified twice (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was told to invite Pharaoh peacefully to follow God's Revelation first, just as the Prophet invited Quraysh, in keeping with the instruction to speak gently.
rows.anchor: Moses was instructed to first invite Pharaoh to follow God’s Revelation, as in 20:44: Yet speak unto him gently

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran teaches that a community is not punished for wrongdoing before receiving guidance through a messenger.
rows.anchor: It is a common Quranic theme that no community is punished for wrongdoing until it has been offered guidance, as indicated in 28:59:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although another account mentions nine clear signs, it does not identify which one was the greatest sign.
rows.anchor: One account mentions nine clear signs (17:101), but does not state which is the greatest sign

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The greatest sign may have been Moses' staff turning into a serpent.
rows.anchor: Some say it is the staff that became a serpent (7:107; 20:66–17; 26:32, 44–45)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The greatest sign may have been Moses' hand turning white.
rows.anchor: the hand turned white (7:108; 26:33; 27:12)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The greatest sign may have been the parting of the sea.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Alternatively, the greatest sign may refer to all the miracles Moses performed.
rows.anchor: or all of the miracles that Moses performed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite the sorcerers recognizing Moses' superiority and the truth of his signs, Pharaoh kept denying them and dismissed the staff and white hand as sorcery.
rows.anchor: Even after Pharaoh’s sorcerers acknowledged the superiority of Moses and the veracity of the signs with which he had been sent

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One view says Pharaoh turned and fled upon seeing the greatest sign or the staff become a serpent.
rows.anchor: Some say that this verse indicates that Pharaoh turned and fled when he saw the greatest sign or the staff turned serpent (R).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another view says Pharaoh quickly devised a plan against Moses after recognizing the power of his message.
rows.anchor: Others say it indicates that, upon realizing the power of Moses’ message, Pharaoh quickly moved to devise a plan against him (R).

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most commentators take Pharaoh's gathering and proclamation as assembling the people to declare his sovereignty.
rows.anchor: Most say this verse indicates that Pharaoh gathered all the people to declare his sovereignty.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Others connect the gathering to 26:53, taking it as Pharaoh summoning his people to pursue the Israelites.
rows.anchor: Others relate this verse to 26:53: Then Pharaoh sent marshalers to the cities, in which case it refers to Pharaoh’s summoning his people

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Several reports say Pharaoh first claimed that he knew no god for his people other than himself, then proclaimed himself their highest lord.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh first said, O notables! I know of no god for you other than myself (28:38), then I am your lord most high

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nakāl also connotes weakness and inability, suggesting God rendered Pharaoh powerless to oppose Moses.
rows.anchor: nakāl, which also indicates weakness and inability, evoking the sense that God rendered Pharaoh impotent in opposing Moses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes punishment in this world and the next; its worldly punishment is commonly taken as the plagues and Pharaoh's drowning with his people.
rows.anchor: many interpret the this-worldly punishment as the plagues sent upon his people and their drowning in the sea

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: A variant reading calls the punishment “of the last and the first.”
rows.anchor: Some read this verse as “the punishment of the last and the first,”

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Under one explanation of that reading, the first punishment answers Pharaoh's claim to know no god but himself, and the last answers his claim to be the highest lord.
rows.anchor: “the first”indicates the punishment for saying, I know of no god for you other than myself

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another explanation assigns the first punishment to Pharaoh's denial of Moses and the last to his claim to be the highest lord.
rows.anchor: others say“the first” is for denying Moses and “the last” is for saying, I am your lord most high (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Sufi account attributed to al-Simnānī contrasts Pharaoh, who saw only himself and forgot God, with al-Ḥallāj, who saw only God and forgot himself.
rows.anchor: In a well-known Sufi interpretation, Alāʾ al-Dawlā al-Simnānī (d. 787/1336) is said to have seen the soul

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One interpretation says the enfolded sun is absorbed into the Divine Throne.
rows.anchor: it may mean that the sun is absorbed into the Divine Throne (Q)

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the sun's light is wiped out.
rows.anchor: that the light of the sun is wiped out (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another interpretation says one part of the sun folds into another before it is rolled up and cast away.
rows.anchor: one part of it will be folded into another and then it will be rolled up and thrown away (IK).

rows.speaker: Hadith
rows.claim: A hadith says the sun and moon will be rolled up on the Day of Resurrection; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: The sun and the moon will be rolled up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early Makkan surah likely followed Sūrah 79, al-Nāziʿāt.
rows.anchor: is an early Makkan sūrah most likely revealed after Sūrah 79, al-Nāziʿāt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Infiṭār is named for the verb in its first verse and belongs to Quranic descriptions of the sky's cataclysmic alteration on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the verb in the first verse, one of the many dramatic descriptions of the cataclysmic alterations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–5 describe Judgment Day events through apocalyptic inversions that turn the ordinary order of heaven and earth inside out.
rows.anchor: a series of apocalyptic inversions in which the normal order both in Heaven and on earth is turned inside out.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–12 reproach and warn people about the Last Day.
rows.anchor: This is followed by a reproach and warning of the Last Day (vv. 6–12).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 13–19 contrast the pious' bliss with the profligate's punishment and show that all will ultimately know how they lived.
rows.anchor: The final section (vv. 13–19) contrasts the bliss of the pious with the punishment of the profligate, indicating that in the end all shall know how they have in fact lived.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two questions may address the Prophet directly, humanity generally, or the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: These verses can be taken as an address directly to the Prophet, to all human beings, or to the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One proposed division addresses verse 17 to the pious and verse 18 to the profligate.
rows.anchor: Some propose that v. 17 is addressed to the pious and v. 18 to the profligate (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Judgment is one on which friends, parents, and children cannot avail one another, leaving each person to rely on their own deeds, intentions, or soul.
rows.anchor: meaning that no individual will have recourse to anything beyond the record of his own actions and intentions, or the state of his own soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Command being with God means every intermediary loses power and God alone acts directly.
rows.anchor: all intermediaries are then stripped of their power, and God alone is the direct actor.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This also points to the passing of all things except God's Face: God remains while everything else fades.
rows.anchor: all things perish, save His Face (28:88), as God abides, while all else fades.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant syntax connects this verse to the preceding question, which then ends after “way.”
rows.anchor: In another variant, this verse can be read as a continuation of the previous verse, in which case the question ends after the word “way.”
